questions.question: How does git branching actually work — and what's a healthy feature-branch workflow with merge vs rebase?
questions.title: Branching Model
questions.direct_answer: A branch is just a MOVABLE POINTER to a commit (41 bytes — that's why branching is instant; commits form an immutable DAG, branches name positions in it). The daily workflow: branch from main → commit early and often → sync with main by REBASE (replay your commits on the new tip — linear history; NEVER rebase pushed/shared branches — it rewrites history others may have built on) or MERGE (a merge commit ties both histories — preserves truth, clutters log). The rule that resolves the debate: rebase LOCAL/unpushed work for clean review diffs; merge into shared branches (most teams' PR merges ARE merges — or squash-merges: one commit per PR, the tidy-but-history-losing default). The safety net: the reflog records every HEAD movement — 'lost' commits are recoverable for ~90 days (git reflog → checkout the tip). Detached HEAD = HEAD pointing at a commit instead of a branch (fine for inspecting, commit-orphans if you work there — branch before committing: git switch -c rescue).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The model + workflow, verified:

```bash
# THE MODEL: a branch = a file holding a commit SHA.
#          commits form a DAG; branches are pointers into it.

git switch -c feat/search          # create + move to a new pointer
# ...work, commit early and often...
git commit -am 'search: skeleton'

git switch main && git pull        # get the new tip
git switch feat/search
git rebase main                    # REPLAY my commits onto the new tip
# history: A-B-C (main) + C'-D' (my work rebased) — LINEAR
# NEVER: rebase a branch others may have pulled — it rewrites SHAs

git push -u origin feat/search      # publish; now it's SHARED — stop rebasing
# PR review → merge (a merge commit ties both histories)

git log --oneline --graph --all     # SEE the DAG
```

Rebase vs merge (the decision, in one line each): MERGE preserves the exact history — 'both branches developed, then tied together' (truthful; the log shows topology; conflicts resolved ONCE at merge time); REBASE rewrites your side onto the tip — 'as if I started from here' (clean linear reads; conflicts re-surface per replayed commit; history is EDITED — the reason it's local-only etiquette). Squash-merge (the PR-button default) = rebase+merge with N commits collapsed to 1 — the tidy option that loses granular history (the trade teams consciously pick).

The recovery tools (the 'I broke it' set): git reflog — every HEAD movement recorded; find the SHA before the disaster, git reset --hard <sha> (local) or git branch rescue <sha> (safe pointer); git reset --soft vs --mixed vs --hard (move HEAD only / unstage too / also delete working-tree changes — the commit-amender's toolkit: --soft + re-commit = amend anything, keep files); git stash push -m 'wip' + stash pop (shelf the dirty tree mid-task); git revert <sha> (a NEW commit undoing an old one — the safe history-preserving undo for SHARED branches vs reset's rewriting).

The professional workflow layer: PRs small (reviewable in minutes), feature branches short-lived (drift compounds), pull BEFORE push when rejected (the push is rejected because the remote moved — pull/rebase first, never --force without --force-with-lease (the guard: rejects if someone else moved the remote since your fetch — the force-push safety belt).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    BR[branch = movable pointer to a commit] --> DAG[commits: immutable DAG]
    LOCAL[local unpushed work] --> RB[rebase onto new main — linear]
    SHARED[pushed branch] --> MG[merge — preserves shared history]
    NEVER[rebase pushed shared branches] --> REWRITE[rewrites SHAs others built on]
    CONFLICT[conflict] --> RB2[rebase: per-replayed-commit]  MG2[merge: once]
    LOST['lost' commit] --> REFLOG[reflog: every HEAD move — checkout the tip]
    SQUASH[PR squash-merge] --> TIDY[1 commit per PR — granular history lost]
    FW[--force-with-lease] --> SAFE[reject stale force-pushes]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The internals that make the workflows make sense: git objects are commits (SHA = content-addressed: tree + parent(s) + author + message), trees (directory snapshots), blobs (file contents), and annotated tags — the DAG emerges from parents. A branch is a ref file (refs/heads/feat) holding one SHA; HEAD usually holds a BRANCH name (attached) or a SHA (detached); 'instant branching' is writing 41 bytes. That model explains everything else: why cherry-pick is a new commit with the same DIFF (new parent = new SHA); why merge finds a base (the DAG's lowest common ancestor) and three-way-merges the changes; why rebase is cherry-picking onto a new base (each replayed commit gets a NEW SHA — the history rewrite).

The working-tree staging model (the two-step commit): working directory → (git add) → index/staging (the NEXT commit's exact content — a real file list, not a diff) → (git commit) → object store. reset's three modes manipulate the index: --soft moves HEAD (index keeps the next-commit state — re-commit anything); --mixed (default) moves HEAD + clears the index (unstaged changes remain in the tree); --hard also resets the tree (destructive — the one that needs the reflog). Interactive staging (git add -p — hunk-by-hunk) is the code-review etiquette tool: separate 'the fix' from 'the drive-by changes' into different commits from ONE dirty tree.

The team-workflow layer (the collaboration norms interviews probe): trunk-based development (small branches merged daily — the CI-friendly extreme) vs git-flow (long-lived develop + release branches — the historical enterprise model now mostly retired); the PR etiquette stack — small diffs, atomic commits (one logical change each: the rebase -i reword/squash/split pass), conventional messages (feat/fix/chore scope — the changelog-generating convention), and NEVER commit secrets (history is forever: a pushed secret needs rotation, not deletion — and git filter-repo is the nuclear rewrite). CI hooks (pre-commit: lint/format/test gates) turn the norms into enforcement — the 'how do you keep a team's git sane' answer is process + tooling, not heroics.
